section: # What This Looks Like From Sénégal
about: Section 15, frozen from the published text (2026-10-17): each unit is a claim, with the words it rests on; a key is a list of alternatives, every key must appear in one paragraph of the draft. Alternatives are added only when a trace calls the new word equivalent. A list's items are keys where an item carries the point; Joel's list rulings (2026-10-03, 10-07: "when there's no actual need for 3 items you can remove one of them") let an item that matters least go, recorded in the draft's fixes file.

units.what: lives in Sénégal, where "intentional community" sounds like a strange Western phrase for what people assume humans already do
the country is unlike anywhere else he's lived
devotional prayers pour into the streets five times a day, and he finds them deeply soothing
Sufi spirituality shows up in everyday life (music, murals, ordinary conversation), not only in designated spiritual spaces; Joel's list rule (10-03, 10-07) lets an item that matters least go
people laugh outside for hours: the most intensely joking culture he's met
he wonders whether he'll ever understand the complicated jokes in Wolof
basic conversation is one thing; knowing why twelve people suddenly cry with laughter is graduate school
in the villages and families he's been around, land, childcare, housing, food and obligation pass through extended family and local memory alongside formal systems
nobody needs a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging": an aunt has already assigned three people a task
even in Dakar, graffiti reads "Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!", and murals of Sufi leaders appear elsewhere
spiritual graffiti still surprises him because he grew up expecting city walls to advertise a product or someone's inability to draw a penis
he won't make Sénégal a surviving communal paradise
the warmth has hard boundaries, and LGBTQ+ people can pay brutally for crossing them
in March 2026, Law No. 2026-08 raised the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to five to ten years in prison
the amended article also criminalizes public "apology" for homosexuality and certain financing or support meant to promote it
the law comes within an existing reality of arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault and mob violence
some say prison actually protects homosexuals from the mob
he won't praise communal belonging while ignoring the people who survive it by hiding who they are, or by leaving
a society can be spiritually alive, generous, funny and intensely communal and still be cruel toward people who violate its accepted categories
community isn't automatically liberating
everything depends on who may belong without pretending
the forgiving social culture has other shadows: people avoid confrontation so thoroughly that everybody knows who stole the sheep and nobody says it aloud
where he lives, neighbors steal his moringa pods every morning; they could plant their own tree; apparently stealing his is more entertaining
everybody raises sheep here, him too, and they're extremely cute
the music, animals, joking, prayer and constant presence of other people can make life feel like another world
the older communal patterns are changing: young people move toward cities, jobs, phones, imported foods and the wider world
men take dangerous sea routes toward Europe
families that once shared nearly everything grow more dependent on cash and individual opportunity
the "Black Tax": when one person starts earning, they're expected to support parents, siblings, cousins, school fees, medical bills, funerals and whoever else the family carries
he understands the instinct: in the ancestral arrangement nobody succeeded alone, and the people who fed, raised, housed and protected you had a real claim on whatever prosperity came through you
sharing wasn't charity; it was how the whole organism survived
the modern version can become soul-destroying because the obligation survived while much of the communal life supporting it disappeared
land, labor, childcare, food and daily belonging are no longer fully shared, but the cash earner may still be expected to carry everybody
the earner struggles to build independence or long-term stability, while relatives receiving money stay dependent because the payments don't create a viable alternative
the ancestral ethic lives on inside an individualistic cash economy, where it keeps people alive while consuming both sides
this is also the boundary problem a money-free commune has to solve
internal life can be cashless while taxes, hospitals, visas, school fees, family obligations, imported tools and other outside relationships still arrive in money

the question isn't recreating individual wages inside the commune but who handles that interface, how much collective cash is kept for it, and how to stop access to outside money from becoming a new status hierarchy
outside work complicates that boundary even before a common purse: it brings another schedule, status system, social world, loyalties and consumption expectations, not only cash
in the first stage an outside earner contributes an agreed share, but money can't buy exemption from ordinary communal work or extra political authority
the group has to notice when outside jobs drain the people and skills needed to build shared livelihoods
otherwise the commune stays a dormitory for the cash economy instead of moving toward a common purse

Zapatista communities faced a version of this with migration: some moved from trying to stop young people leaving to negotiated arrangements in which migrants work elsewhere while keeping defined communal obligations
the conflict between mobility and belonging didn't disappear; it became something the community could name and negotiate
Westerners often begin with isolation and try to rebuild tribe; many Africans begin with inherited communal life and watch parts of it dissolve
urban Africans interested in intentional community may come to it after feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left
this makes it a global conversation, not a Western lifestyle niche
living villages hold knowledge no book can reproduce, but they're living people, not exhibits
go respectfully, contribute something, learn the language, and don't arrive expecting a spiritual service package
his own residency process in Sénégal was inexpensive and straightforward
French and Wolof matter much more than English
the ideal of Teranga, hospitality, is real in his life: he stays in a friend's family house, and they refuse rent
that generosity exists beside watchfulness, social conservatism, bureaucracy and the ordinary complications of a real country
